requirements.requirement: The system should render correctly in common web browsers used by companies, including older browsers, without layout issues.
requirements.source_citation: People use normal web browsers — desktops mostly, but sometimes laptops or tablets. The UI should just render correctly in the common browsers companies use, and not fall apart when someone has, like, an older browser. We try to keep the HTML and CSS fairly standard so it’s broadly compatible. I mean, it’s annoying when layouts break, so we try to avoid that.
requirements.rationale: The stakeholder explicitly mentions the need for compatibility with common browsers and the importance of avoiding layout issues. This indicates a clear usability concern related to browser compatibility.
requirements.follow_up_question: What specific versions of browsers should be supported, and are there any known issues with particular browsers?

requirements.requirement: The system should log exceptions with stack traces and context, and provide a mechanism to send these logs back for analysis.
requirements.source_citation: It should definitely log exceptions — stack traces, context, whatever — and keep a record the ops or our support team can pull. Ideally the app will capture enough info so we can reproduce and fix the issue, and there’s a mechanism to send those logs back for analysis rather than leaving them scattered on a single server, because, well, people move servers and you lose context.
requirements.rationale: The stakeholder provides a detailed description of the logging requirements, emphasizing the need for comprehensive exception logging and centralized log management for debugging purposes.
requirements.follow_up_question: What specific logging framework or tool is preferred for this purpose?

requirements.requirement: The system should feel snappy and handle peak usage times without performance degradation, and should scale as the company grows.
requirements.source_citation: It just needs to feel snappy, honestly — waiting around kills productivity. Heavy operations should be quick. Also mornings and right before big meetings are when the most people hit it, so it needs to not choke during those peaks. And we want it to scale forward a bit as the company grows, not be a one-off that flails when usage increases.
requirements.rationale: The stakeholder explicitly mentions the need for snappy performance, handling peak usage times, and scalability as the company grows, indicating clear performance and scalability concerns.
requirements.follow_up_question: What specific performance metrics or benchmarks are expected for peak usage times?

requirements.requirement: Access to the system should be controlled, integrating with company identity systems or approved account lists, and audit trails should be maintained.
requirements.source_citation: Access needs to be controlled. Mostly it’s company employees, and then occasionally external partners who’ve been set up with approved accounts. We shouldn’t be letting random people in, so integration with whatever company identity system or approved account list is important. Also audit trails are useful when someone says, 'Hey, why was my meeting moved?'
requirements.rationale: The stakeholder emphasizes the need for controlled access and integration with company identity systems, as well as the importance of audit trails for security and accountability.
requirements.follow_up_question: What specific identity systems or protocols should the system integrate with?

requirements.requirement: The codebase should follow common design patterns and best practices to ensure maintainability and ease of future feature additions.
requirements.source_citation: We try to follow common design patterns and best practices so the codebase is predictable, not some custom spaghetti. That makes it easier for someone new to jump in and add a feature without undoing half the app. I mean, I’ve been the new person before and it’s awful when nothing is documented or consistent.
requirements.rationale: The stakeholder explicitly mentions the importance of following design patterns and best practices for maintainability and ease of future development.
requirements.follow_up_question: Are there any specific design patterns or coding standards that should be followed?

requirements.requirement: The system should handle locale and timezone settings correctly to avoid scheduling issues, and error messages should be clear and non-cryptic.
requirements.source_citation: For example, once we had a site where the calendar times were off because of a weird local DB setting and two teams ended up double-booked and, uh, it got awkward with coffee spilled during a scramble to move people. That taught us to pay attention to locale and timezone handling and to make the error messages less cryptic.
requirements.rationale: The stakeholder provides a specific example of a past issue related to timezone handling and the importance of clear error messages, indicating a usability concern.
requirements.follow_up_question: What specific timezone and locale settings should be supported?

requirements.requirement: The system should be customizable to support client branding and multiple languages, and should be accessible with keyboard navigation and screen reader support.
requirements.source_citation: Yeah, it should be customizable so clients can put their branding on it and it should support multiple languages. Accessibility is important too — keyboard navigation and screen reader friendliness — because different offices have different needs and we don’t want to exclude people.
requirements.rationale: The stakeholder explicitly mentions the need for customization, multilingual support, and accessibility features, indicating a clear usability concern.
requirements.follow_up_question: What specific accessibility standards or guidelines should be followed?

requirements.requirement: The system should be tested against a representative set of browsers to ensure compatibility.
requirements.source_citation: We do some testing against a representative set of browsers; teams generally run it through the ones they care about. I don’t run the whole matrix myself, but the idea is that it shouldn’t be a mystery which browsers will work — we try to cover the ones users rely on.
requirements.rationale: The stakeholder mentions testing against a representative set of browsers, indicating a usability concern related to browser compatibility.
requirements.follow_up_question: What specific browsers and versions should be included in the testing matrix?

requirements.requirement: The system should be flexible to work with different database systems as preferred by the IT team.
requirements.source_citation: It depends on the client site, really. Some places have big enterprise databases, some have lighter databases sitting in the office. We’ve had to make the code work with whatever the IT team prefers, so the app can talk to different database systems; I’ve been fixing little compatibility quirks as they come up.
requirements.rationale: The stakeholder explicitly mentions the need for flexibility to work with different database systems, indicating a portability concern.
requirements.follow_up_question: What specific database systems should the application be compatible with?
